title: Add TCP Health Check using SYN, SYN-ACK, and RST packets
body:
### Welcome!

- [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on [GitHub](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues) and didn't find any.
- [X] Yes, I've searched similar issues on the [Traefik community forum](https://community.traefik.io) and didn't find any.

### What did you expect to see?

I have implemented a new TCP health check functionality using the `tcp-shaker` library (https://github.com/tevino/tcp-shaker). This improvement uses SYN, SYN-ACK, and RST packets to perform more accurate health checks for TCP services.

You can review the implementation on my branch [here](https://github.com/reporter/traefik/tree/dev).

Would love to get feedback and discuss how this can be integrated into the project.

Thanks!

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Some related issues are #5598 and #1657.

To use it, the procedure is as follows:

```yaml
services:
  example_tcp_service:
    loadBalancer:
      servers:
        - address: 10.42.64.4:7445
        - address: 10.42.0.1:7445
        - address: 127.0.0.1:8448
      healthCheck:
        path: /health
        interval: "10s"
        timeout: "3s"
        mode: tcp
```

Note that the `path` is ignored due to the nature of the TCP protocol.

Additionally, it would be interesting to consider a `mode: passive`, which enables passive checks based on observing communication with back-end nodes. However, this is not as straightforward.

This proposal is just what I am looking for!

It covers these two cases:

- proxying a HTTPS server from downstream with TLS passthrough
- reundant TCP services

The first case is common in environments in which you have your own certificates that you must present to upstream. This is common in non-cloud environments, which host public services, but use a proxy to mask the origin IP source.

I am looking to migrate to traefik to replace Caddy and nginx, which I have to both use currently for the following reasons:

1. Caddy does not support TCP proxying
2. nginx requires a Plus subscription for monitoring TCP endpoint metrics via Prometheus

The proposal in this thread would provide a feature which would make traefik a one-stop solution for my multiple use-cases.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Hi @participant1, 

Thank you for your input, and I appreciate the opportunity to clarify. 

I haven’t submitted a PR yet because I’ve never contributed to Traefik before, and I’m unsure if my implementation meets Traefik’s standards. I wanted to gather feedback before formalizing the contribution. 

The main difference between my implementation and the one by @participant5 is the approach to sending `SYN` and `SYN-ACK` packets. My implementation leverages the `github.com/tevino/tcp-shaker` library, which allows sending these packets directly to the kernel without passing the request to the application. As a result, these connection attempts don’t appear in the logs, which I believe is an advantage in terms of cleaner operation and reduced noise in monitoring.  

Initially, my implementation performed a regular TCP connection, as seen in [this commit](https://github.com/reporter/traefik/commit/b80ce22626cb1b462a43b0d56f21b7a9533713e5#diff-2c565121f665a1bc64eef7d8aeb4c3c406473167bb5fb93426755d18c98fa204L173 ). However, I moved away from that approach because it closely resembles what I believe @participant5’s implementation does — opening a full TCP connection and waiting for a response.  

From my perspective, this approach is not ideal. TCP is typically used as a transport layer for higher-level protocols, so expecting a meaningful response at this level doesn’t align with its intended use. For instance, if a response is expected, it should ideally use a protocol like HTTP. This behavior aligns more with what HAProxy does, which focuses on using TCP for its core purpose without conflating it with application-level expectations.

I’d be happy to collaborate further to refine the solution and ensure the best approach for Traefik. Let me know how you’d like to proceed!

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
I'm going to summarise things up, as well as add my thoughts. If one of my assumptions is wrong, please correct me. Also I'm not a maintainer or involved in traefik in any way, but I would like to see a TCP Health Check feature in traefik. Therefore trying to help with this a bit.
It looks like, we are talking about these two implementations:

## Approaches
@participant5 
1. Establishing a complete tcp connection: `Syn, Syn/Ack, Ack`
- What happens with the established connection? Is it kept open, for how long, some data send, immediately closed (client and server send Fin/Ack, Fin/Ack)?
- So basically a full three way handshake for the connection and a two way handshake for the termination?
- Are you using any external go package for that/ external dependencies?

@reporter 
2. You are using the `tcp-shaker` package to only do a: `Syn, Syn/Ack, Rst`

- Which means, as soon as the server replies with the Syn/Ack, the connection is terminated via `Rst`?
- `Rst` is definitely send after Syn/Ack? Or could it be, that the package simply does a `Syn, Syn/Ack` without sending a `Rst` which would result in what, a server waiting - for the length of a timeout - until the `Rst`/ usually `Ack` arrives? Which would basically lead to a wasted connection.


## Information/ Collection of statements

A comment states that:
```
"... I got from some expert that it is usually done for improve performance since it will have less handshake than normal connection. ..."
```
> https://serverfault.com/questions/884982/is-rst-ack-expected-in-a-tcp-health-check


Fortinet seems to do `Syn, Syn/Ack, Rst` (although they just write `Syn, Syn/Ack`)
```
Layer 4 TCP and UDP health checks are "liveness" checks. At Layer 4, FortiADC sends health check probes and attempts to connect to a specific TCP or UDP port. A TCP SYN request to port 80, for example, would expect a TCP SYN ACK response in return. If the response is not received within the configured timeouts and intervals, port 80 would be marked DOWN for that server, or server instance.
```
> https://help.fortinet.com/fadc/4-2-2/html-e/Content/Health_Checks/TLHC_L4_HC.htm


Tencent cloud is doing `Syn, Syn/Ack, Rst`
>https://www.tencentcloud.com/document/product/214/6097#tcp-.E5.81.A5.E5.BA.B7.E6.A3.80.E6.9F.A5


Envoy, not really sure as “connect only” TCP health checking could mean both.
```
If “receive” is an empty array, Envoy will perform “connect only” TCP health checking. During each cycle, Envoy will attempt to connect to the upstream host, and consider it a success if the connection succeeds. A new connection is created for each health check cycle.
```
> https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/upstream/cluster_manager/cluster_hc


HaProxy uses `Syn, Syn/Ack, Rst`
```
these sequences of packets including a RST are completely normal. This is the way that haproxy uses to do health checks efficiently. As soon as haproxy has discovered that the endpoint is up, there is no point in wasting any further resources at either end. It turns out that using TCP RST is the most efficient way for kernels at both ends of the connection to finish their conversation and free up those resources.
```
> https://discourse.haproxy.org/t/connection-reset-seen-every-2-sec-haproxy/2156/5

Radware Alteon
```
The TCP handshake flow is SYN, SYN/ACK and RST like the example of packet captures below shows.
```
> https://support.radware.com/app/answers/answer_view/a_id/1028668/~/alteon-tcp-health-check-without-sending-ack


## Summary
It makes sense to say that `Syn, Syn/Ack, Rst` is the more efficient implementation, as it terminates immediately, no waiting on timeouts, no connections kept open for longer than needed. Also it looks like, others use exactly that approach (see link collection above).
Me personally, I don't like external dependencies and would say, avoid them as much as possible. Could `Syn, Syn/Ack, Rst` be achieved with go standard libraries (without a lot of extra/ duplicate work)?

@participant1 what are your thoughts on this? Which one of these two approaches would you/ other maintainers prefer and why?

```
1. SYN
```  

comments.author: participant7
comments.body:
@reporter I really like how you did the health check, for us the TCP part is not really required but I decided to make changes on your PR to make it useful for our scenario. 

https://github.com/reporter/traefik/pull/1

In PostgreSQL HA clusters managed by Patroni, only the current leader is writable, and its status is exposed via a local HTTP API (returning HTTP 200 for the leader, 503 for replicas). Existing Traefik TCP health checks only verify port availability and will try to run the http healthcheck with an incorrect scheme, which is insufficient for routing exclusively to the active leader node or simply doesn't work.

Previously, setups had to rely on HAProxy or custom external health-checkers to bridge this gap. This PR allows Traefik to natively perform HTTP health checks on TCP backends, eliminating the need for external tools and keeping the entire proxying logic within Traefik.

What's changed
A existing healthCheck options allowed specifying an HTTP endpoint (host, port, path, status code) for a TCP service. They were just never used. Now we override the port, path and schema for the health check on this service

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Hi everyone, and thanks to @participant7  for reactivating this important discussion. I'd like to share my technical perspective on the best path forward, which has always been grounded in using the right tool for the right job.

From my point of view, Traefik should offer two clear and distinct modes for TCP service health checks:

1. The Pure TCP Check (mode: tcp): For verifying raw port availability, the `SYN, SYN-ACK, RST` handshake is the industry standard. It's lightweight, fast, and unambiguously answers the question: "Is a service listening on this port?". My original implementation in PR #10794 using `tcp-shaker` achieves exactly this. It's crucial to note that this approach does not introduce any new dependencies to the project, as `tcp-shaker` leverages libraries already present in Traefik's vendor tree.

2. The Application-Layer Check (`mode: http`): There are valid use cases, like the Patroni HA cluster example, where a simple port check is insufficient and an application-level response must be validated. The solution for this already exists within Traefik and it's brilliant: using `mode: http` on a TCP service's health check. This elegantly decouples the health check mechanism from the data plane routing, allowing the use of the powerful, existing HTTP checker to verify paths, status codes, etc., for any service that exposes an HTTP endpoint for its status.

Given these two clean and correct paths, I strongly believe that adding application-level logic (like payloads or initial handshakes) directly into the TCP health checker itself would be a step in the wrong direction. It creates a hybrid, non-standard mechanism that tries to replicate functionality we already have in a more robust and appropriate form.

I have been successfully running both of these configurations in my own environments. My recent contributions to [tcp-shaker](https://github.com/tevino/tcp-shaker/pull/31) were also aimed at ensuring the underlying tooling remains solid and maintainable.

@participant1, to move this forward, I propose that we officially adopt this philosophy of two distinct, clear modes. I am fully available to help finalize this feature, whether that means reviving my original PR or collaborating on a new one that implements these well-defined principles. The goal for all of us is to provide the community with a robust, well-designed, and easy-to-maintain solution.

Thanks!!

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Hello @participant1, thank you for the clarification on the proposed path forward.

I understand the desire to merge things in sequential steps to maintain order. However, I share the architectural concerns raised by @participant7.

My main concern is that merging PR #11238 with its current architecture (a separate `TCPHealthChecker`) would force us to introduce a significant and breaking refactor in the very next PR. We would essentially be merging a design that we know we need to replace immediately.

From my perspective, a unified **`ServiceHealthChecker`** is the most robust long-term solution. Here's why:

1.  **Follows the DRY Principle (Don't Repeat Yourself):** It avoids code duplication, which is critical for long-term maintainability. More duplicated code means a larger surface for bugs and higher maintenance costs.
2.  **Enables Critical Features:** The recently discussed ability to run an **HTTP health check on a TCP service** (`mode: http`) is a perfect example. This feature inherently requires sharing logic with the HTTP checker, making a separate TCP checker architecturally unviable.

Regarding scope, the primary goal should be to integrate a pure TCP check via `tcp-shaker` (`SYN/ACK`). If the team later wants to add more complex checks, like inspecting N bytes or sending specific payloads, that could perfectly be handled as a **new, separate `mode` in the future**. The unified checker architecture provides the ideal foundation for this.

**My Proposal:**
Instead of a two-PR approach, I suggest we implement the unified architecture directly within the existing PR #11238.

I have been reviewing the latest changes in Traefik (up to `v3.5.0`), and I'm ready to help adapt my implementation to fit into @participant5's branch following this unified structure. This would allow us to merge the right architecture from the start, saving everyone significant time and rework.

What are your thoughts on this approach? I believe it addresses your goal of moving forward while ensuring we build on a solid and maintainable foundation.

comments.author: rtribotte
comments.body:
Hi,

Thanks for all your feedback!

@reporter The review of #12138 is now done.
The approach of duplicating the HeathChecker and adapt it for TCP, to us, looked to be the best way to go as of now.
The reason is not only how the healthcheck mechanism is configured and conducted, but also the need for using, on HTTP side, the roundTripper of the service, and on the TCP side, the dialer of the service.
Additionally, we considered the possibility of adding later a new TCP check mode (SYN, SYN-ACK, and RST packets), and nothing prevent that with this design.

@participant7 After second thoughts about you contribution to @reporter branch, to allow HTTP healthcheck with TCP services, we think it worth opening a dedicated issue to track this need and know more about the community traction on this.
Could you please open a dedicated issue.
Design wise, we think the split approach doesn't prevent introducing such a feature.
